name: Minaean
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Ancient South Arabian, unvocalized epigraphic corpus (Arbach 1993 is lexicon); stress unrecoverable/undescribed.

new_statements.quote: 4:7 Closely connected with the phenomenon just mentioned is the appearance of a "parasitic" h within a syllable. Rhodokanakis, on the basis of a parallel feature in the MSA dialects, deduces (18) that a strongly accented vowel tended first to diphthongize, then to split into two vowels, between which a glide was finally introduced. In ESA, this feature is particularly characteristic of MIN (31:11, 33:2, 40:38). [...] [33:2:] explains the appearance of the h in this position as due to a strong accent falling on a case-ending when a pronominal affix or second dependent genitive is added

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (mina1279 has no catalog record and no stress statement held by the project). Compatible with what the mirror's records from Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224 (Minaean parasitic h 'thought.. caused by a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)') and Nebes & Stein 2008: 149-150 (no conclusions possible on accentual relationships): Beeston supplies the underlying hypothesis (accent on case-ending/ultima before suffixes, on the fem. pl. ending; first-syllable accent in bhn-, bhnt) but no placement rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated anywhere: the query luzac+beeston+epigraphic+stress returns 0 hits, i.e. the word 'stress' does not occur in the scanned, and 'accent' occurs only in five places, all explaining the Minaean 'parasitic' h. Following Rhodokanakis, a strongly accented vowel diphthongized and split into two vowels with a glide (h) between them; Beeston uses this to posit, for Minaic, a strong accent on the case-ending / ultimate syllable of a noun when a pronominal affix or dependent genitive (or qualifying clause) follows (genitive -h/-hy; long forms of the affixes), a strong accent on the external feminine plural ending (-ht), and a regressive accent on the first syllable in bn/bnt (stem bhn-) and bhnt 'daughters'. These are reconstructive hypotheses for particular morphological contexts, not a description of where word stress falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned in the passages read
new_statements.exceptions: §31:11: bhnt 'daughters' (R 3699/4 etc.) lacks the -ht ending because 'the accent fell on the first syllable.. and the ending was consequently unaccented and the parasitic h did not arise'; §4:8: outside MIN the parasitic h is rare and often otherwise explicable.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern epigraphic Minaic = Minaean = Madhabic (Beeston's dialect siglum MIN; Höfner's 'Minäisch'), the Ancient South Arabian language of the Jawf (Ma'in, Qarnaw, Yathill) and of the Minaean colony at Dadan/al-'Ula, 8th-1st c. BCE; DASI splits it into Central and Marginal Minaic. Beeston and Höfner are grammars of Epigraphic South Arabian as a whole with dialect-specific paragraphs; the accent passages quoted are the Minaean-specific ones.

new_statements.quote: [§25] ... gezeigt, daß auch im ASA. dieses nichtetymologische h auf einen ursprünglichen zweigipfligen Akzent zurückgeht. Bei Vokalen, die einen derartigen Akzent hatten, entwickelte sich zunächst zwischen den beiden Tongipfeln ein Gleitlaut, der gewöhnlich h war. [...] [§28] Die Diphthonge in -hw, -hmw haben zur Voraussetzung, daß die Suffixe einen starken Akzent hatten, und zwar die Pluralsuffixe auf der Ultima. Für das Zurückweichen des Akzentes vom Suffix, das in den anderen asa. Dialekten z. T. schon weit fortgeschritten ist (siehe gleich später im Min. und Qatab.), finden sich also im Sabäischen erst wenige Spuren
new_statements.translation: [§25] ... shown that in ASA too this non-etymological h goes back to an original two-peaked accent. In vowels that had such an accent a glide, usually h, first developed between the two tone peaks. [...] [§28] The diphthongs in -hw, -hmw presuppose that the suffixes carried a strong accent, the plural suffixes on the ultima. Of the retraction of the accent from the suffix, which in the other ASA dialects is in part already far advanced (see below on Minaean and Qatabanian), Sabaic accordingly shows only few traces.
new_statements.citation: Höfner, Maria. 1943. Altsüdarabische Grammatik (Porta Linguarum Orientalium 24). Leipzig: Harrassowitz.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, no statement held by the project). Consistent with Beeston 1962 (same Rhodokanakis hypothesis: strong/two-peaked accent behind Minaean parasitic h) and with Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224 and Nebes & Stein 2008: 149-150 as recorded in the mirror accent not directly recoverable). Höfner's 'retraction of the accent from the suffix' in Minaean and Beeston's 'strong accent on the ultimate syllable of the noun' before affixes describe the same configuration (accent immediately before the suffix), so no contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule of word-stress placement is given (probes for Betonung, Wortakzent, Wortton, Pänultima find nothing; §4: the vocalization of ASA is known only by analogy with North Arabic and Ethiopic). §25 'Akzent', as far as read, adopts Rhodokanakis: the non-etymological ('parasitic') h, chiefly Minaean, reflects an original two-peaked (circumflex-like) accent on a vowel, which developed a glide h between the peaks and split into a disyllabic group (v > vv > vhv). §28: the ASA pronominal suffixes originally bore a strong accent, the plural suffixes on their ultima (Sabaic -hw, -hmw); retraction of the accent off the suffix is 'already far advanced' in Minaean and Qatabanian (§30: in Min. 'Enttonung und Verkürzung' of the singular suffix); an earlier Lautlehre passage: 'der starke Akzent, der auf dem Suffix ruhte.. konnte wohl auch zu Wortverkürzungen führen'; §100 (traces of case inflection, Minaean genitive): head noun and following determination were spoken under one accent lying at the end of the construct chain. All of this is reconstruction from orthographic h, not an attested stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned in the passages read (the 'zweigipfliger Akzent' is a two-peaked accent on one vowel, not secondary stress)
new_statements.exceptions: dialect differences only: accent retraction from the suffix advanced in Minaean and Qatabanian, barely begun in Sabaic (§28); p. 28 of §25 was not read, so any qualification there is unknown

BCE; DASI splits it into Central and Marginal Minaic. Beeston and Höfner are grammars of Epigraphic South Arabian as a whole with dialect-specific paragraphs; the accent passages quoted are the Minaean-specific ones.

Lists only Stein 2011 (subclassification) and Arbach 1993; alternative names Madhabic, Minaic, Epigraphic South Arabian.

Says the phonology was essentially like the other Old South Arabian languages and notes the unexplained non-etymological h in nominal endings/pronouns/particles; contains no information on vowels, stress or accent. Cites Kogan & Korotayev 1997 and Nebes & Stein.

sources.note: Secondary reports read: Höfner 1943 §25 says Rhodokanakis (Studien I, S. 12-56), on the parallel of Modern South Arabian and above all Soqotri, showed 'daß auch im ASA. dieses nichtetymologische h auf einen ursprünglichen zweigipfligen Akzent zurückgeht' (a two-peaked, i.e. circumflex/pitch-type accent on the vowel, between whose two 'Tongipfel' a glide h developed); Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224 summarise the same view as 'caused by a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)'. This is the only accentual/pitch hypothesis in the Minaic literature; the work itself was not opened.
